10Training & RL

The skills aren’t written, they’re trained.

ⓘ Notes
The skills aren’t written, they’re trained: first self-study “guess the next word” on huge amounts of text, then learn formats from demonstrations, and finally polish with rewards and preferences.

Why it’s designed this way: Rules can never be written out in full, but examples and feedback can be unlimited; let the model work out the patterns from data itself.

Watch a neural network “learn” to draw a boundary Sample data

Artificial neural networkA mathematical function with lots of “knobs”: numbers in, numbers out, with the knobs tuned automatically from data.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

No hand-written rules — give it examples and let it find the patterns itself; the structure is general and works on almost any data.

✅ Why this works

With non-linear activations, stacked layers can approximate very complex functions; gradients make “which way to turn” computable.

⚠️ Limits / notes: It learns statistical correlations, not causal understanding; it’s hard to interpret; “neuron” is just a biologically inspired name.

Artificial neuronWeighted sum + activation: the smallest unit of computation.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

The weighted sum expresses “how important each input is”; the activation introduces a “bend”.

✅ Why this works

Many “kinked lines” put together can approximate curvy shapes.

⚠️ Limits / notes: A single neuron can only draw a straight-line boundary.

Backpropagation + gradient descentWorks out which way each parameter should move, then takes a small step.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

With billions or even hundreds of billions of parameters, hand-tuning is impossible. The chain rule efficiently computes each parameter’s “responsibility” for the error (how big an effect and in which direction), at a total cost of only a few times the forward computation.

✅ Why this works

Like walking downhill blindfolded: each time, take a small step in the steepest downhill direction underfoot; repeat many, many times and the loss keeps going down.

⚠️ Limits / notes: It doesn’t guarantee finding the “global minimum”, only heading downhill nearby; but for large networks it works very well in practice, and why is still being researched.

Loss (cross-entropy)A single number: how badly this question was guessed.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Billions of parameters need one shared goal, ideally “a single number”: the smaller the better, so that “which way to adjust” makes sense. Use the negative log of the correct word’s probability: as the probability approaches 1 the loss approaches 0; as it approaches 0 the loss grows; being wrong and very confident is punished hardest.

✅ Why this works

Paired with softmax, the gradient is especially clean: the adjustment to each word’s score = predicted probability − correct answer (1 or 0). This signal neither explodes nor vanishes, and its size reflects exactly how wrong it was.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Cross-entropy is the most common choice and makes sense from the viewpoint of probability and information theory, but it isn’t the only possible loss.

Architectures: MLP / CNN / RNN / TransformerHow neurons are connected: different wiring suits different data.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

An architecture hides “prior assumptions” about the data; when they fit the data, it needs less data and generalizes more easily.

✅ Why this works

The Transformer assumes the least, performs generally well when data is plentiful, and suits GPU parallelism extremely well.

⚠️ Limits / notes: There is no absolute best, and the boundaries are blurring (hybrid architectures, new sequence models and so on are being explored).

③ Details · why

Self-supervised learning

No human labels needed: the answer is hidden in the data.

“To be or not to ___” → the answer “be” is right there in the original text.
Turn every position in a sentence into an exercise, and one article becomes hundreds or thousands of practice questions.
Pretraining

“Guess the next word” on huge amounts of text, producing the base model.

③ Details · why

Supervised fine-tuning (instruction tuning)

People write “question → high-quality answer” pairs, and the model learns the format and habits from them.

{"user": "Will it rain in Hangzhou tomorrow?",
 "assistant": {"tool_call": {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Hangzhou", "date": "tomorrow"}}}}
(Example: one fine-tuning record that “teaches the model when to call a tool”)
LoRA

A budget fine-tuning method that trains only a “thin patch”.

③ Hands-on demo

Reinforcement learning

Learns to make decisions through “trial and error + reward”, aiming to maximize the long-term cumulative reward.

Q-learning

Estimates a long-term score Q for every “state + action” and corrects it after each step.

Mini maze: an agent learns to walk on its own with Q-learning Sample data

  • 🤖 starts at the bottom left
  • 🏁 goal +10, 🕳️ trap −10, −0.1 per step
  • dark cells are walls.
  • Cell colour = the cell’s best Q value (green = good, red = bad), arrow = the best direction learned so far, and the small number in the bottom-right corner is the cell’s largest Q value.
  • At first everything is 0 and it knows nothing.
Episodes 0
Steps per episode (lower is better, max 100):

Observe: in the first few episodes it bumps around, the cells near the goal turn green first, and then the “good news” gradually spreads back towards the start; with enough training the step count drops close to the shortest path. With ε at 0 it may get stuck on a sub-optimal route.

🧪 You be the labeller: which answer is better? Sample data

Question: “Will it rain in Hangzhou tomorrow?”. Tap the answer you prefer. The reward model adjusts its scores accordingly; the policy (the LLM) then leans towards higher-scoring answers, but a KL constraint stops it from drifting too far at once.

Preference alignment (RLHF etc.)Has people compare “which answer is better” and uses those preferences to adjust the model.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

A “good answer” is hard to write down as rules or demonstrations, but people find it easy to compare which of two answers is better.

✅ Why this works

Comparison data is cheap and consistent; the reward model compresses that feeling into a function that can score automatically, enabling optimization at scale.

⚠️ Limits / notes: The model may learn to flatter, ramble, or sound confident without being right (reward hacking); human preferences themselves are subjective and biased.

Reward modelLearns to imitate human preferences and scores answers.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

People can’t score millions of answers in real time, so a “stand-in judge” is needed.

✅ Why this works

Generalizes a limited number of human comparisons to answers it has never seen.

⚠️ Limits / notes: When the reward model has loopholes, the policy will exploit them (reward hacking).

KL constraintA brake that says “don’t stray too far from the original model”.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Chasing reward alone makes the model weird (saying strange things to farm points).

✅ Why this works

Keeps the original language ability and knowledge, fine-tuning only in the direction of “more agreeable”.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Too large a coefficient and it can’t learn; too small and it easily drifts.

DPO (direct preference optimization)Adjusts the model directly with “A is better than B” data, without training a separate reward model.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

The process is simpler and more stable, needing neither online sampling nor a separate reward model.

✅ Why this works

Turns a reinforcement learning problem into something like supervised learning, which is much easier to engineer.

⚠️ Limits / notes: It relies on fixed preference data and can’t improve while exploring the way online RL can; which method is better depends on the scenario.

Reasoning RL (verifiable rewards)For problems like maths and code where right and wrong can be checked automatically, let the model try several times and reward it when it’s right.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

The reward is objective (right is right), so it isn’t easily fooled by “flattery” and can be trained at scale with confidence.

✅ Why this works

Through lots of trial and error the model discovers for itself which ways of thinking are more likely to succeed, rather than just imitating steps written by people.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Mainly applies to domains with clear right and wrong; the model may “guess the right answer with wrong reasoning” or game the test cases; the written-out reasoning doesn’t necessarily reflect the internal computation faithfully.

③ Details · why

Massive data + next-word guessing

The training exercises: cut a passage from text and guess the word that follows.

Data and compute

The two fuels of training: huge amounts of high-quality data + large GPU clusters.

Self-supervised learning

Makes exercises from the data itself, without human labelling.

“Scaling laws” (bigger models, data and compute work better) are an empirical trend distilled from many experiments; they hit diminishing returns and are not laws of physics.

🧪 Learning rate and overfitting: fitting a curve

ⓘ Sample data: 10 training points + 40 validation points

  • Why it’s built this way: Training means “taking small steps in the direction the error decreases”.
  • Too small a step (learning rate) and it barely moves
  • too big and it overshoots the valley or even flies off.
  • A model that is too simple can’t learn the pattern (underfitting)
  • one that is too complex memorizes the noise too (overfitting).
  • That’s why a set of “unseen questions” (the validation set) is kept for checking.
👀 Try this:
  • degree 1 → underfitting (a straight line can’t fit the curve)
  • degree 3–4 → just right
  • degree 9 + long training → overfitting (the curve passes through every blue dot, but the orange validation error goes up).
  • Drag the learning rate all the way right → divergence.
  • When it overfits, try setting weight decay to 0.01.
🧪 LabQ-learning

🧪 RL maze: you place the walls, traps and rewards

ⓘ Q-learning, 7×7 grid

  • Why it’s built this way: Many tasks have no “model answer” to imitate
  • you only “find out whether it was good by doing it”.
  • RL lets an agent learn by trial and error, passing “the good news from the goal” back one cell at a time — but it only cares about the reward, so if the reward design has a loophole, it will exploit it.

👀 Try this:
  • train 500 episodes first and see the arrows point to the treasure
  • put a wall in the way, train again and watch it detour.
  • Put a 🍪 (+1, doesn’t end the episode, grows back after being eaten) near the start: it may prefer farming points next to the cookie over going for the treasure — that is “reward hacking”, which is why rewards must be designed to match the real goal.
